title: Reasonable, not right
subtitle: Unfair dismissal II: the fairness test in practice
objectives: State the Burchell test for conduct dismissals and explain what each of its three limbs requires the employer to show
Explain the 'range of reasonable responses' standard and why a tribunal must not substitute its own view of what it would have done
Apply the Burchell test and the Polkey deduction to a fact pattern, distinguishing a substantively unfair dismissal from a procedurally flawed one that would likely have happened anyway

leadingAuthorities.citation: British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell [1978] IRLR 379
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the three-limb test tribunals apply to conduct dismissals: genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation

leadingAuthorities.citation: Iceland Frozen Foods Ltd v Jones [1982] IRLR 439
leadingAuthorities.role: States the 'range of reasonable responses' standard and warns tribunals against substituting their own view for the employer's

leadingAuthorities.citation: Polkey v A E Dayton Services Ltd [1988] AC 344
leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that a procedurally unfair dismissal can still attract reduced compensation if a fair process would likely have led to dismissal anyway

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Lesson 5 gave you the gateway and the reason; this lesson is where most of the marks in an unfair dismissal problem question actually live, because 'was it fair' is rarely a one-line answer. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can state Burchell — this lesson checks whether you can run all three limbs against real facts, not just recite them.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards scenarios where one Burchell limb is satisfied and another isn't: expect to have to say which one fails, not just whether the dismissal was fair overall.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state all three Burchell limbs separately before moving on — later parts assume you already have them as a checklist, not a vague impression.

overview.hook: A tribunal member is privately convinced the dismissal in front of them was too harsh — they'd never have sacked the employee for this. Under the test this lesson teaches, that private conviction is close to irrelevant. Unfair dismissal law doesn't ask a tribunal to decide what it would have done. It asks whether the employer's decision fell within a range that a reasonable employer could have reached — a standard built, deliberately, to stop tribunals rewriting management decisions from the armchair of hindsight.

parts.heading: From 'what reason' to 'was it fair'
parts.voice: structural — bridges from Lesson 5's gateway into this lesson's real question
body: Lesson 5 established the gateway: qualification, then a potentially fair reason the employer must show under s 98(1)–(2). None of that answers the question that actually decides most unfair dismissal cases — was dismissing for that reason fair, given everything the employer knew and did?

That second stage is governed by s 98(4) ERA 1996, which asks whether the employer acted reasonably or unreasonably in treating the reason as sufficient to dismiss, 'in the circumstances (including the size and administrative resources of the employer's undertaking)', judged in accordance with equity and the substantial merits of the case. Notice what this section does not say: it does not ask whether the tribunal itself would have dismissed. It asks whether the employer's decision was one a reasonable employer, in that employer's position, could have reached.

This lesson works through how that broad statutory test has been given shape by case law for the most heavily litigated dismissal reason — conduct — and then generalises the underlying standard, before turning to what happens to compensation when a dismissal is unfair for procedural reasons alone.

components.definition: The statutory test asking whether the employer acted reasonably in treating the established reason as sufficient to dismiss, given the circumstances including the employer's size and resources — assessed objectively against what a reasonable employer could have decided, not what the tribunal itself would have decided.

interaction.prompt: Under s 98(4) ERA 1996, what is the tribunal actually asked to assess?
options: Whether the employer acted reasonably in treating the reason as sufficient to dismiss
Whether the tribunal itself would have dismissed the employee on the same facts
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The test is objective reasonableness by the employer's standards, not a re-run of the decision through the tribunal's own preferences.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Section 98(4) asks about the reasonableness of the employer's decision, not what the tribunal itself would have done — that second framing is exactly the substitution error the case law in this lesson exists to prevent.

parts.heading: The Burchell test: three questions, one at a time
parts.voice: reference-style — a checklist part students return to before every conduct problem
body: British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell concerned an employee dismissed for suspected dishonesty — discrepancies in staff discount transactions pointed to theft, though nothing was ever proven to a criminal standard. The Employment Appeal Tribunal used the case to lay down the framework tribunals still apply to conduct dismissals founded on suspected misconduct, and it has three separate limbs, each of which must be satisfied.

First, did the employer genuinely believe the employee was guilty of the misconduct? This asks about the employer's actual state of mind at the time of dismissal, not what turns out to be objectively true. Second, did the employer have reasonable grounds for that belief, based on what was known at the time? Third, had the employer carried out as much investigation into the matter as was reasonable in the circumstances? All three limbs must be met; an employer who genuinely and reasonably believed the employee guilty, but never bothered to investigate properly, still fails the test.

It is worth being precise about what Burchell does not require: it does not require the employer to prove misconduct to a criminal standard, or even prove it happened at all. This is a civil, reasonableness-based test about the process and state of mind behind the decision, not a re-trial of guilt.

components.label: The Burchell test
points: Limb 1 — genuine belief: did the employer honestly believe the employee committed the misconduct?
Limb 2 — reasonable grounds: was that belief based on reasonable grounds, given the information available at the time?
Limb 3 — reasonable investigation: had the employer carried out as much investigation as was reasonable in the circumstances?
All three limbs must be satisfied — failure on any one limb is enough to make the dismissal unfair on this ground

components.caseName: British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell
components.factsShort: An employee was dismissed for suspected dishonesty involving staff discount transactions, following an internal investigation but no criminal conviction.
components.ratioShort: A conduct dismissal for suspected misconduct is fair only where the employer genuinely believed the employee guilty, on reasonable grounds, following as much investigation as was reasonable in the circumstances.

expanded.facts: Discrepancies were found in staff purchase records suggesting the claimant had been involved in dishonest transactions using her staff discount. The employer investigated, formed a belief in her guilt, and dismissed her. No criminal proceedings established guilt to a criminal standard.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Employment Appeal Tribunal held that in cases of suspected misconduct, the employer need not prove the employee actually did what is alleged. What must be shown is a genuine belief in the employee's guilt, formed on reasonable grounds, after an investigation reasonable in the circumstances of the case.
expanded.significance: Burchell remains the standard framework applied to conduct dismissals founded on suspected misconduct decades later, and its three limbs are treated as close to a checklist in tribunal practice and in exam answers alike — though later cases refined how the 'range of reasonable responses' standard (Iceland Frozen Foods) applies to each limb, rather than treating Burchell as a mechanical tick-box exercise.

interaction.prompt: Put the three Burchell limbs in the order a tribunal works through them.
items: Did the employer genuinely believe the employee was guilty of the misconduct?
Was that belief based on reasonable grounds available at the time?
Had the employer carried out as much investigation as was reasonable in the circumstances?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence — belief, then the grounds for it, then the investigation behind it. All three must hold; a gap at any stage is enough to fail the test.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The order runs from the employer's state of mind (genuine belief), to what justified that belief (reasonable grounds), to how it was arrived at (reasonable investigation) — not the other way round.

parts.heading: The range of reasonable responses
parts.voice: argumentative — states the tempting counter-view before Iceland Frozen Foods forecloses it
body: It's natural, reading a set of dismissal facts, to form your own view of whether the punishment fit the conduct — and equally natural to think a tribunal should do the same. Iceland Frozen Foods v Jones explains, carefully, why that instinct has to be resisted.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal in that case set out the standard now applied throughout unfair dismissal law: in judging the reasonableness of an employer's decision to dismiss, the correct approach is not to ask what the tribunal itself would have done, but whether the decision to dismiss fell within a 'band' or 'range of reasonable responses' that a reasonable employer might have adopted. Different reasonable employers, faced with the same misconduct, might reach different decisions — one might dismiss, another might issue a final written warning — and both could be within the range. The dismissal is only unfair if it falls outside that range altogether, not merely because the tribunal would have chosen differently.

This standard applies not only to the decision to dismiss itself, but to each stage of the process — including, on the authority developed since Burchell, whether the investigation was reasonable. It is a genuinely deferential standard, and it is the single biggest reason unfair dismissal claims are harder to win than students initially expect: the employer doesn't have to be right, or even to have made the best decision available. It has to be within the range a reasonable employer could have reached.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often analyse a dismissal by asking 'was this too harsh a punishment for the conduct?' and treating their own answer as the test.
components.whyItsWrong: That question substitutes the student's (or the tribunal's) own view for the objective range-of-reasonable-responses standard. The correct question is whether a reasonable employer could have dismissed for this conduct — not whether dismissal was the best or most proportionate response available.

interaction.prompt: Tap the phrase in this tribunal reasoning that correctly applies the range of reasonable responses standard.
interaction.scenarioText: The tribunal noted that, while it personally would have issued a final written warning rather than dismissing, it found that dismissal for this conduct fell within the range of responses a reasonable employer could have reached, and therefore was not unfair.
tappableSpans: it personally would have issued a final written warning
dismissal for this conduct fell within the range of responses a reasonable employer could have reached
interaction.correctSpan: dismissal for this conduct fell within the range of responses a reasonable employer could have reached
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the correct legal test being applied. The tribunal's own preference (a warning instead) is expressly set aside as irrelevant — what matters is whether dismissal itself sat within the band a reasonable employer could have chosen.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sentence stating the actual legal test, not the tribunal's personal view. The tribunal's own preference for a lesser sanction is exactly what Iceland Frozen Foods says must not decide the case.

parts.heading: Procedural fairness, and what happens when it fails
parts.voice: direct — separates substance from process before introducing Polkey
body: Fairness under s 98(4) has both a substantive dimension (was the outcome — dismissal — within the range of reasonable responses?) and a procedural one (was the process followed before reaching that outcome fair?). A dismissal can be substantively justified on the facts but still unfair because of how it was carried out — no proper investigation, no disciplinary hearing, no chance for the employee to respond to the allegations, or no right of appeal offered.

This raises an obvious question: if the outcome would probably have been the same even with a fair process, should compensation still be paid in full for a dismissal that was flawed only procedurally? Polkey v A E Dayton Services Ltd answers this directly. Mr Polkey was made redundant with no warning and no consultation, in breach of what a fair procedure required — but there was a real possibility that, even with proper consultation, he would still have been selected for redundancy.

The House of Lords held that a failure to follow a fair procedure will generally render a dismissal unfair, even if the employer reasonably (if wrongly) believed consultation would have made no difference — procedural fairness is not optional just because the employer is confident of the outcome. But at the remedy stage, if a tribunal finds that a fair procedure would probably still have led to dismissal, or would have led to it at a later date, compensation can be reduced accordingly — potentially to a very small figure, or even to nil, reflecting the likelihood that dismissal would have happened anyway. This is the 'Polkey deduction'.

components.text: Where the employer has fulfilled the requirements of subsection (1), the determination of the question whether the dismissal is fair or unfair (having regard to the reason shown by the employer) — (a) depends on whether in the circumstances (including the size and administrative resources of the employer's undertaking) the employer acted reasonably or unreasonably in treating it as a sufficient reason for dismissing the employee, and (b) shall be determined in accordance with equity and the substantial merits of the case.
elements: Reasonableness is assessed by reference to the employer's own circumstances, including its size and resources
The test covers both the decision to dismiss and the process followed to reach it
Assessed in accordance with equity and the substantial merits of the case, not a fixed checklist alone

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that an employer's honest belief that consultation 'would have made no difference' excuses skipping a fair procedure altogether under Polkey?
sliderLabels: Definitely does not excuse skipping it
interaction.explanation: Polkey rejected exactly this argument at the liability stage: a fair procedure must generally still be followed, even where the employer is confident of the outcome. That confidence only becomes relevant later, at the remedy stage, where it can justify a reduction in compensation rather than a finding that the dismissal was fair.

parts.heading: Putting substance, process and remedy together
parts.voice: reflective — closes by rehearsing how the three doctrines interact in one problem
body: A well-built unfair dismissal answer, once the s 98 gateway is cleared, keeps three questions distinct rather than blurring them into a single verdict. Was the employer's genuine belief in guilt reasonably grounded and reasonably investigated (Burchell, for conduct cases)? Did the ultimate decision to dismiss fall within the range of responses a reasonable employer could reach (Iceland Frozen Foods)? And, separately again, was the process itself fair — and if not, would a fair process probably have changed the outcome (Polkey)?

These three questions can point in different directions within a single case. An employer might have entirely reasonable grounds and a proportionate outcome, but have skipped a disciplinary hearing — substantively fine, procedurally unfair, and a strong candidate for a substantial Polkey reduction rather than full compensation. Conversely, a scrupulously fair process can still produce a substantively unreasonable outcome if the underlying decision falls outside the range a reasonable employer could reach.

Keep this three-part structure explicit in any problem answer: state which limb of Burchell (if conduct is the reason), whether the outcome sits within the range of reasonable responses, and whether any procedural failure would attract a Polkey deduction rather than defeating the compensation claim altogether.

components.definition: A reduction — potentially to nil — in an unfairly dismissed employee's compensatory award, applied where the tribunal finds that a fair procedure would probably still have resulted in dismissal, reflecting the likelihood of that outcome rather than excusing the procedural failure itself.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is a Polkey deduction the more likely outcome, rather than a finding that the dismissal was fair overall?
interaction.scenarioA: An employer dismisses an employee for gross misconduct after a full, reasonable investigation and a properly conducted disciplinary hearing at which the employee was able to respond, and the decision to dismiss was well within the range of reasonable responses.
interaction.scenarioB: An employer dismisses an employee for gross misconduct with reasonable grounds and a proportionate outcome, but never holds any disciplinary hearing or gives the employee any opportunity to respond before deciding to dismiss.
interaction.explanation: A describes a dismissal that is fair both substantively and procedurally — no deduction needed, because there's no unfairness to remedy. B is substantively sound but procedurally flawed (no hearing, no chance to respond), which is unfair, but likely attracts a significant Polkey deduction if a fair process would probably have reached the same result.

testPool.prompt: Name the three limbs of the Burchell test for conduct dismissals.
acceptableAnswers: genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation
testPool.modelAnswer: Genuine belief in the employee's guilt; reasonable grounds for that belief; and as much investigation as was reasonable in the circumstances.

testPool.prompt: Does the Burchell test require the employer to prove the alleged misconduct to a criminal standard?
options: No — it requires a genuine, reasonably grounded and reasonably investigated belief
Yes — the employer must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt

testPool.prompt: Which of the following correctly states the range of reasonable responses standard from Iceland Frozen Foods v Jones?
options: A dismissal is unfair whenever the tribunal itself would not have dismissed
A dismissal is unfair only if it falls outside the range of responses a reasonable employer could have reached
A dismissal is fair provided the employer followed some kind of process, regardless of outcome
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option is exactly the substitution error Iceland Frozen Foods warns against — the tribunal's own preference is not the test. The third option ignores that the standard applies to the outcome, not just to whether some process happened; a process can be followed and the outcome can still fall outside the reasonable range.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a tribunal follows in a contested conduct dismissal, from Burchell through to remedy.
items: Assess whether the employer genuinely believed the employee guilty, on reasonable grounds, after reasonable investigation (Burchell)
Assess whether the decision to dismiss fell within the range of reasonable responses (Iceland Frozen Foods)
If the process was procedurally flawed, ask whether a fair process would probably still have led to dismissal (Polkey)
Determine the compensatory award, applying any Polkey deduction

testPool.prompt: Under s 98(4) ERA 1996, what factor does the statute expressly say should be taken into account when assessing the reasonableness of the employer's decision?
options: The size and administrative resources of the employer's undertaking
The employee's personal financial circumstances
Whether the employer has been sued for unfair dismissal before
testPool.explanation: Section 98(4) expressly directs attention to the circumstances, 'including the size and administrative resources of the employer's undertaking' — a small business is not held to the same procedural standard as a large one with a dedicated HR department.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below summarising Polkey, highlight the sentence stating what happens to compensation where a fair procedure would probably have led to dismissal anyway.
testPool.passage: The House of Lords held that a failure to follow a fair procedure will generally render a dismissal unfair, even where the employer reasonably believed consultation would make no difference. However, where the tribunal finds that a fair procedure would probably still have resulted in dismissal, the compensatory award may be reduced accordingly, potentially to nil.
testPool.ratioSentence: where the tribunal finds that a fair procedure would probably still have resulted in dismissal, the compensatory award may be reduced accordingly, potentially to nil

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly causes this employer to fail the third Burchell limb (reasonable investigation), even though it may have a genuine and reasonably grounded belief.
testPool.scenarioText: The employer genuinely believes the employee stole from the till, based on a discrepancy in the day's takings that several other staff also had access to. Rather than reviewing CCTV footage or interviewing any other staff with access, the employer dismisses the employee the same day based solely on the discrepancy.
tappableSpans: genuinely believes the employee stole from the till
several other staff also had access to
Rather than reviewing CCTV footage or interviewing any other staff
dismisses the employee the same day
testPool.correctSpan: Rather than reviewing CCTV footage or interviewing any other staff
testPool.explanation: This is the investigative failure. Genuine belief (limb 1) may well be present, and the discrepancy might arguably support some grounds (limb 2), but failing to pursue readily available evidence — CCTV, other staff with access — when other people plainly had opportunity too is exactly the kind of gap that fails the reasonable investigation limb.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more clearly falls outside the range of reasonable responses, rather than within it?
testPool.scenarioA: An employee is dismissed for a first instance of minor lateness (arriving ten minutes late once), with no prior warnings, no pattern of poor timekeeping, and no disciplinary process at all.
testPool.scenarioB: An employee is dismissed for a third instance of serious lateness after two prior written warnings, following a proper disciplinary hearing.
testPool.explanation: A is a stark, one-off, minor issue met with the most severe sanction and no process — realistically outside any range a reasonable employer could have reached. B, by contrast, shows an escalating, warned, and procedurally sound response to a repeated problem, well within the range even if a different employer might have given one more warning.

testPool.prompt: A tribunal finds an employer had reasonable grounds and conducted a reasonable investigation, but never gave the employee a chance to respond to the allegations before deciding to dismiss. What is the most accurate description of the likely outcome?
options: The dismissal is fair overall, because two of the three Burchell limbs were satisfied
The dismissal is unfair for lack of procedural fairness, but compensation may be reduced under Polkey if dismissal would probably have happened anyway
The dismissal is automatically fair provided the reason itself was genuine
testPool.explanation: Denying the employee any opportunity to respond is a serious procedural failing that itself renders the dismissal unfair, regardless of how sound the substantive grounds were. The employer's strong substantive case becomes relevant at the remedy stage, through a possible Polkey deduction, not at the liability stage.

testPool.prompt: Nadia is dismissed for gross misconduct after her manager receives an anonymous tip that she falsified a client invoice. The manager, convinced by the tip alone, dismisses her the next day without speaking to Nadia, reviewing any documents, or holding any meeting. Analyse whether Nadia's dismissal is likely to be fair.
factsToOrder: The allegation comes from a single anonymous tip
The manager is convinced by the tip alone
No documents are reviewed and no meeting is held
Nadia is dismissed the next day with no opportunity to respond

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Nadia's dismissal for suspected gross misconduct is fair, applying the Burchell test and the range of reasonable responses.
modelAnswer.rule: A conduct dismissal for suspected misconduct is fair only where the employer genuinely believes the employee guilty (limb 1), on reasonable grounds (limb 2), following as much investigation as was reasonable in the circumstances (limb 3); the ultimate decision must also fall within the range of responses a reasonable employer could reach, and a fair process (including a chance to respond) is generally required.
modelAnswer.application: The manager may genuinely believe the tip (limb 1 arguably satisfied), but an uncorroborated anonymous tip, acted on without checking any documents, is unlikely to amount to reasonable grounds (limb 2), and no investigation of any kind took place (limb 3 clearly failed). Nadia was also given no opportunity to respond before the decision was made, which is an independent procedural failing.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The dismissal is very likely to be unfair: it fails limbs 2 and 3 of Burchell, and separately fails procedural fairness by giving Nadia no opportunity to respond before the decision was taken.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a Polkey deduction can reduce compensation all the way to nil?
sliderLabels: Not confident — some award is always payable
Confident — it can be reduced to nil
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — it can be reduced to nil
testPool.explanation: Correct. Where a tribunal finds that a fair procedure would probably still have resulted in dismissal, the Polkey deduction can, in principle, reduce the compensatory award all the way to nil — the dismissal remains unfair as a matter of liability, but the loss actually caused by the unfairness can be assessed as none.

testPool.prompt: An employer genuinely and reasonably believes, after a thorough investigation, that an employee committed gross misconduct, and dismisses. A different, equally reasonable employer might have issued a final written warning instead. Is the dismissal unfair?
options: Yes — because a final written warning was also a reasonable option, dismissal must have been too severe
Not necessarily — provided dismissal itself fell within the range of responses a reasonable employer could reach, it can be fair even if other reasonable employers would have chosen differently
Yes — automatically, because Burchell requires the least severe sanction available to be chosen
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think that because a lesser sanction was also reasonable, the harsher one must therefore be unreasonable — but the range of reasonable responses standard expressly allows for more than one reasonable outcome on the same facts. Burchell says nothing about choosing the least severe sanction; it governs belief and investigation, not the choice of penalty.

testPool.prompt: Which case establishes that a tribunal must not substitute its own view for that of the employer when assessing reasonableness?
options: British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell
Iceland Frozen Foods Ltd v Jones
Polkey v A E Dayton Services Ltd
testPool.explanation: Iceland Frozen Foods Ltd v Jones is the authority for the range of reasonable responses standard and the warning against tribunal substitution. Burchell governs belief and investigation in conduct cases; Polkey governs the effect of procedural failure on compensation.

testPool.prompt: An employer skips a disciplinary hearing entirely before dismissing an employee for conduct, but the tribunal later finds the outcome would have been identical even with a full, fair process. What is the correct legal outcome?
options: The dismissal is unfair, but the compensatory award is likely to be reduced significantly, potentially to nil, under Polkey
The dismissal is fair, because the outcome would have been the same regardless

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'was this the right decision' as the test, rather than 'did this fall within the range a reasonable employer could reach' — and, separately, assuming that a confident employer can skip a fair process because the outcome seems obvious. Polkey punishes exactly that assumption at the liability stage, even though it can soften its cost at the remedy stage.
